Purpose — why we're gathering

Build shared strategy and craft, together

The Gathering Pre-Read · Read before Sunday

Pre-Read: Mission, Landscape & Where We Stand

How DM currently understands its mission, where it will actively invest, and where it needs to constrain. Please read in advance so everyone joins the pop-up with a shared starting point.

Open the Pre-Read Deck
”

How to read this. Several sections are flagged as open, since the pre-read's own point is to invite scrutiny, not present a finished view.

Why this pre-read exists

Acknowledging our context, before getting into mission and strategy.

One feature of DM's current system: many threads of work, driven by many different people. That has real benefits — no overreliance on any one partner, resilience to shocks, the ability to adapt as we learn, external accountability, and capacity for leadership from across the team. It also has real downsides — embedded fragmentation, difficulty finding coherence, bandwidth overstretch, and a harder path to building big, deep things through to follow-through.
The funding reality

Public sector funding is notoriously insufficient, slow and piecemeal. Philanthropy has helped create the conditions for bolder, larger-scale funding — but it's mostly project-based, 1–2 years at most, and can't be relied on long-term as the majority model.

Where core funding helps

Core funding such as JRF and QCF builds more coherence — but the underlying business model is still public- and philanthropy-funded and project-based, until DM can unlock recurring revenue or other forms of investment and private capital.

To be relevant at the scale of the crisis gap will require organising resource and creativity at a different scale — and capital that recognises DM's work in ways neither the public nor private sector alone can currently sustain.

How the team will use this material

Different roles need different degrees of strategy resolution — designed for mission-holders, project-holders and pathways-builders alike.

Cumulative — built up over time
  • Golden threads — consistent themes across all our work
  • Stories — about us, our best and our not-best
  • Ambitions — the outcomes we want to make happen
  • Insights — lessons learnt on constructing strategy well
Cyclical — refreshed twice a year
  • Signals from the future that determine relevance
  • A trajectory to organise central energy and DM-level fundraising around
  • A landscape we can play within
  • Investment areas DM can financially back with its own resources

Together, these inform the various strategies driven by people and teams across DM in response to their own conditions — held together by a learning system that's still in development.

Mission Pathways — aims

Aim

Relevance

Increased relevance to planetary risk and world realities.

Aim

Assets

Increased quantum and quality of assets to do the work — relationships, capital, reputation, partnerships.

Aim

Distribution

Better distribution of asset-raising and holding across the team — funding, influence, reputation, relationships.

Golden threads

DM's driving question, held loosely: what does it take for communities and societies to remain able to live, flourish and exercise real agency in a world of increasing systemic instability? DM's mission is to drive and share insight into this question so the wider field can act on it.

This question is drawn from a lot of data and team insight, but hasn't yet had sufficient scrutiny to be confirmed as the question.

Meeting societal risks

Uncover what's actually relevant to avert unfolding crises and influence the politics to meet it — bridging horizons from what could be conceptually to what can be done now.

Open learning, power-with

A focus on the capacity of the field beyond DM itself — sharing learning openly as standard, outcome-sharing and power-with partnerships that go beyond service contracts.

Multi-agent innovation

Not government- or corporate-driven solutions, but mass, multi-agent, multi-capital means and capacities.

The dark matter

A focus on the invisible underlying systems which, at scale, have meaningful relevance to the size of the risk — with particular technical competence here.

Entanglement & relationality

Inspecting the philosophies that drive everything — how we understand what it means to be human and in relationship with the world — and strengthening the relational field.

What we bring to the table

A relentless commitment to the unfolding risks facing people, and to what it would actually take to chart — and picture — an alternative path. A posture of co-holding the mission and outcomes with partners across the full space of enquiry. Expertise in surfacing the "dark matter" that shapes what's deemed possible, and the underlying philosophies that code it — paired with the multi-disciplinary capacity not just to propose alternative routes but to help structure the conditions that make them real, including through DM's own resourcing.

"What do you bring to the table? That seems to be a positioning question external partners ask of DM."
— Team comment, 10x100 Q2 2026

Insights on building strategies that land

Our reputation — a first AI-assisted read

By dimension
  • Very strong: intellectual originality; trust among EU, UN, city & philanthropic partners
  • Strong: systems-design & experimental capability; ethical integrity, no material public controversy
  • Moderate–strong: practical instruments & adoption, concentrated in a few projects
  • Moderate–weak: independently quantified long-term outcomes
  • Weak–moderate: clarity about what DML actually is
  • Underdeveloped: organisational identity beyond Indy Johar
  • High risk: founder-dependency
By audience
  • Systems-change practitioners: very high regard
  • Regenerative economics circles: influential, thought-leading
  • Public innovation labs: respected collaborator
  • Civic tech / design communities: innovative, experimental
  • Traditional business operators: often too abstract
  • Venture / startup ecosystem: not commercially oriented
  • Grassroots activists: mixed — visionary, sometimes elite
"A highly respected frontier systems-change lab with strong intellectual influence, admired for ambition and originality, but sometimes criticised for abstraction and unclear pathways to scalable implementation."
— Summary: high credibility, incomplete legibility, under-consolidated proof
2026 Patterns picks this apart further — see Pattern 3, "funders buy proof now"

Strategy insights from across the team

Requisite variety

The variety within a system must be at least as great as the variety of the environment it's responding to — in tension with the desire for focus and simplicity.

Resonance

We don't attract what we want — we attract what we are.

Gödel's incompleteness

We can't think our way out of a system using the mind that built it.

Dialogic strategy

The best strategies form dialogically with the field, funders and partners. Advanced alone, they often quickly die.

Follow-through

Idea → weaving & implementation → reflection & feedback, with real closure — then going again.

Spread & focus

The recurring shape underneath almost every pathway: a broad exploratory phase before conditions allow narrowing into demonstration.

Builder + driver + enabler

Healthy pathway work needs all three — rarely present in one person: pathway building, operational drive, and condition/team enablement.

Projects-per-person

Often correlates inversely with efficacy — ultimately a business model and resourcing question DM hasn't fully solved.

A maturity ladder for funding

Growth Pot → XCO pre-seed → tooling/demonstration fund is a potential progression, designed and now being tested. Explicit staging can serve as intentional gates for review and validation.

Spin-in / spin-out as an endgame

Mature initiatives can "spin in" to their own legal entity under the DML Group while still drawing on DM's protocols and backend (RZ is the current example), or spin out fully independently. This reframes DM's role: less a single delivering organisation, more an ecosystem orchestrator.

DM's own capital as catalytic

When DM brings its own capital (e.g. RZ, XCO) into an early-stage partnership, it can unlock conditions that wouldn't otherwise exist — but seemingly only when staged as an escalating, mutual commitment.

Demonstration changes everything

At the point anything reaches real-world demonstration, ecosystem orchestration — and everything that requires — becomes critical.

The craft of pathways building

Build the field, conversation & demand first — 6–9 months before needing the resource Only move one step adjacent to real experience — geography, capability, or domain Always hold more than one option; single-option positions are too vulnerable The first excited funder is rarely the finisher Learning transmitted weekly & daily is the greatest strategic asset The posture you build a relationship with is the posture that embeds — hard to change later Write the summaries, minutes, provocations — that's often where the real strategic work happens Relationship-holding is itself a strategic asset; insincerity shows quickly Field-building requires an external posture — internal focus alone caps you

DM-level fundraising

DM's next large-scale fundraise is organised into three connected layers — each also a constraint/prioritisation function.

Funded

XCO

Where a proven position becomes an actual investable deal.

Emerging

Coordination tooling

Tooling that lets multiple actors align, commit, and follow through on an entangled position. No dedicated resourcing yet — possible pathway through QCF.

Unfunded

The precursor layer (Dm Next)

Where a position gets found and shaped before either of the above is possible — the layer DM has always worked in, running on borrowed time and unallocated capacity rather than a funded structure of its own.

!

The throttle. DM now has the conditions and relationships to raise significant funds, but lacks the strategic readiness to move it with integrity to the commitments that would require. Unlikely to get another tranche after raising £50–100m — the money has to move well enough to catalyse other economies. Our current throttle is more strategy than fundraising.

2026 Patterns has more on this — see Pattern 6, "funders under pressure," and Pattern 1, "winning less on open bids"

Season recaps — how DM got here

2016 – 2019

Season 1

Started within 00 as a 5-person experiment (Indy, Eunji, Jack, Chloe, Carlotta). Project-based grants and contracts. Began with provocation blogs, talks and invitations. Identified system mapping, alternative financing, multi-agent collaboration and blockchain-secured smart contracting as emerging tech — with an assumption those stacks couldn't yet be funded together, so DM focused on "dark matter" components instead. Key work: UNDP Istanbul Innovation Days, Legitimate Cities, A Smart Commons, TreesAI.

2019 – 2022

Season 2

Grew to 25 (2019), then 60 (2021). First standalone entity in the Netherlands, then Canada, South Korea, Sweden and UK. EU work became 60%+ of income. Main work: Healthy Clean Cities, UNDP Cities. By 2021, sought to reduce EU-funding reliance; TreesAI boomed with Google's Impact Accelerator. By season's end: a longing for real-world prototypes — "system demonstrators" identified as the key unit needed.

2022 – 2025

Season 3

Stable at 60–70 people; project + core funding, with Laudes funding critical infrastructure. Matrix established to make sense of the portfolio. Realised System Demonstrators are hard to fund directly — DM could only play enabling roles. New opportunities opened: NZC, Planetary Civics, Life-ennobling Economics, 7 Gen Cities, Cornerstone Indicators, Many-to-Many contracts, CircuLaw, Permissioning the City. Some Labs (DmCS, Beyond the Rules) secured core funding and began to consolidate.

2025 – present

Season 4

Stewards and Health Keepers established via the Governance Gap Committee — a major governance shift. Funding sources now include investment alongside grants and core funding. Still discovering: Civilisational Options as a sharper driver for demonstration investment, and a tooling fund aimed at a clear stack of tools for civic innovation. This is the season we're in now.

"We laid out this ambition for season 3 to transition from a 'starburst' portfolio in discovery, to choosing where to invest and build with intention. On hindsight, we underestimated what it would take to really architect this throughout the organisation, and our governance system was a barrier to that."
— Indy & Annette, on DM's story, May 2026

Pre-Read, continued · Read before Sunday

Seven Patterns from 2026 Pathway Building

What we're actually sensing across our own calls, our pathways database and our own docs this year — what it means for us, and the open question each one leaves. Read alongside the main Pre-Read; several of the deep dives on Monday connect straight back to these.

”

Shape of each pattern: what we're sensing → what it means for us → the open question. All seven come from our own calls, our own pathways database and our own docs — not external benchmarking.

01

We're winning less on open bids

What we're sensing

Open calls used to be a huge reliance for us, and our success rate on them has dropped off — partly, we suspect, because anyone can write a convincing application now with AI. Meanwhile most of our successful pathways this year came from relationships already in the field: a follow-on from prior work, an invitation, a partner organisation wanting to do something with us.

What it means for us

As the pathway building circle, we should be more intentional about whether open calls are really worth the effort for the conversion rate we've had this year. Energy shouldn't go into crafting big calls unless we're uniquely positioned or we've already been invited in.

Open question

What's our test for entering an open call? A starting hunch: do we already hold the funder or the consortium lead? Is there a framework or direct-award route to the same buyer instead? Do we have someone who can carry it through to contract, not just to submission?

02

Saying no matters — and so does agreeing what we're saying yes to

What we're hearing

Some good refusals this year: stepping back from the Laudes consortium, which led to Laudes seeing us as an ecosystem thinking partner rather than a grantee. "I'd much rather not take the money than take a liability." A £250 thank-you to a collaborator rather than opening a consultancy relationship. A hard-won lesson from Helsinki that we can't manufacture co-funding by discounting ourselves. What we don't have is any shared basis for those calls — good individual judgements, made individually.

What it means for us

The step beyond "say no more often" is agreeing what we actually want from a partner, and how we distribute our capacity across the partners we've got. Without that, every no is a personal call, and every yes competes with every other yes for the same people.

Open question

What are we looking for in a partner, and who decides when capacity moves from one to another?

03

Funders buy proof now — and proof is our weakest line

What we're hearing

Our own assessment, from the pop-up pre-read: intellectual originality very strong, trust among EU, UN, city and philanthropic partners very strong — but independently quantified long-term outcomes moderate–weak, and clarity about what DML actually is weak–moderate. Evidence of practical instruments and adoption is moderate–strong, "but concentrated in a few projects." Partners keep asking the same two questions: "What do you bring to the table?" and "What is the clear value proposition that Dm brings?"

What it means for us

The one to put the most weight on — and it connects directly to Pattern 1. If we're spending less unfunded time writing applications, the obvious place for that time to go is evidencing what we've actually built: a website that clearly shows what we've built and what changed as a result; impact made legible as specific, checkable claims rather than a report; and progress shown as it happens, so the people we want investment from can watch it developing rather than being told about it afterwards.

Open question

If we deliberately moved a chunk of the unfunded time currently going into applications into evidencing our work — who holds that, and what would we build first?

04

We're increasingly getting paid to set things up

What we're hearing

Four pieces of work this year followed the same steps without anyone connecting them: map a field → find the innovations in it → run a structured process with the people in it → help launch a fund or vehicle at the end — Homes, FreeHouse, and XCO among them. One Steward is running a version of it for the JRF Unfurling Fund. And a funder offered to convene UK housing funders on our behalf, so they could converge their own funding streams. In all of these, we're the organiser rather than the deliverer.

What it means for us

Everything we price, we price in days. A day rate works when we're doing the work — it doesn't fit designing a fund, convening a room of funders, or holding an accelerator, so that work tends to land on our books as unfunded time even when it's the most valuable thing we did.

Open question

Is there another way to be paid for setting things up — a stewardship retainer, a convening fee, a share of what gets mobilised? Someone in the room has probably already been offered one of these and turned it into a day rate.

05

Handovers need to get cleaner

What we're hearing

Three of the projects that went over budget this year share a pattern: seeded the same way, project holder changed more than once, timeline stretched. What was promised to the partner never reached the people delivering it, and the team over-delivered because the relationship mattered.

What it means for us

Not a skills problem — a short protocol. What was promised, at what price, with what latitude, and who can authorise going over.

Open question

Whose job is that, and where does it live?

06

Some of the funders we rely on are under pressure themselves

What we're hearing

This isn't only about us getting better or worse at fundraising — the organisations we depend on are dealing with their own changed conditions, and want to see co-funding or match-funding to de-risk.

What it means for us

An irony worth naming: one major funder wants funding diversification from us for exactly the reason we want it from them — everyone is de-risking at the same time. Two things follow. Match funding isn't a bonus any more, it's the entry condition — a proposal that arrives without other money attached is arriving incomplete. And a funder relationship is less durable than it used to be; two years now looks like the honest maximum to plan against.

Open question

Not resolved yet.

07

Demand is shifting between areas of work, not just shrinking

What we're hearing

It's easy to read this year as "there's less money." Looking across the pathways database and the calls, what's actually happening is that money is moving between areas.

Getting easier to fund
Housing & built environment4% → 6% → 25%

"Very easily fundable and gathers the right people much more easily." Multi-year funding secured, plus several local authorities and a six-figure programme start.

Risk, resilience & security4% → 4% → 9%

Fund managers now hiring a "Head of Systemic Risk." A small risk clinic abroad opened conversation with major climate philanthropies. Risk and security named in our own pre-read as a "meta frame" driving investment priorities we hadn't previously envisaged.

AI, digital & civic tech5% → 6% → 12%

A major tech funder at interview stage on a seven-figure ask, plus several smaller digital-agency and indicators partners.

Food systemsrising

Camden's early-stage grant with a follow-on in the millions crystallising this autumn. Food and soil read as where the "hot money" is — money to the ground, easy to implement.

Oceans & blue economyrising

"Easier to go from philanthropy to impact with return."

Getting harder to fund (less certain — our pathway database is weak here)
Nature-based solutions & green infra finance10 → 4 pathways

"Even though we can show the numbers, it still doesn't mean that you can get people to invest — there's no regulated market for anything else but carbon."

Broad, everything-at-once framingsdown

Named directly as the challenge of securing "blanket funding" for an initiative spanning both social and planetary agendas — portfolio-level framing asks funders to hold too much complexity at once.

System demonstratorsdropped as a frame

Dropped in our own pre-read "because lack of political economy to fund."

Diagnosis & framing workthe one to underline

One partner's concern about a live piece of work was that it had "stayed primarily in the diagnosis and solution space and needs to advance to testing viability." That's the demand shift in a sentence: funders want the thing tested, not the thing named.

Open question

Where is demand growing that we already have the credibility to move into — and what would we have to stop doing to have the capacity to go there?

Closing circle

Ten overviews, roughly 20 minutes each, back to back in one room — nobody's choosing a track, everyone hears everything. Three open Spaces and lunch break up the day; that's deliberate, not dead time. Swap the order if it fits the room's actual energy better — the point is that everyone's together and the deep work happens in the Spaces, Tuesday, Wednesday and the gaps in between, not squeezed into today.

The overview format

Every session runs the same tight two-part structure — long enough to actually land, short enough that ten fit in a day.

1

What it is, and why it matters now (10 min)

The lead frames the piece of work: what it is right now, and how it connects to DM's driving question and golden threads. Group listens without interrupting.

2

The live question for the room (10 min)

Lead asks one sharp, honest question they actually want help with right now — not a rhetorical one. Room offers what it's got. There isn't time here for the full working session; that's what the Spaces, and the rest of the week, are for.

”

What the Spaces are for. Three times through the day, the room gets 20 minutes with no fixed agenda — to go back to whichever session had real energy, ask the harder follow-up, pull two threads together, or just sit with something a bit longer. This is also where craft signal tagging happens: each person adds a card for the one craft a piece of work is actually testing right now (e.g. "structuring complex partnerships," "political economy — what will people get behind"). Cards go on the wall — raw material for the afternoon's convergence, and for deciding where Tuesday, Wednesday and the gaps in between actually go deep.

The ten pieces of work

A working frame and tailored prompts for each piece of work — more than any 20-minute overview can cover live. Use them to prep the overview itself, and again in the Spaces, Tuesday, Wednesday or wherever the conversation actually continues. Where there's already real texture on the work (Homes That Don't Cost the Earth, Camden Food Mission, Beyond the Rules & Many-to-Many), the prompts pull from that directly. Where the material on the table is lighter, the prompts are built from DM's own patterns and are flagged as a starting point for the lead to sharpen.

Sharing Work Through the Lens of a Place: Spain

Session 1

A place-based lens on DM's work as it's showing up in Spain — pulling the live threads there into one shared picture rather than treating them as scattered, unconnected engagements. Not yet fully scoped for this session; the value is in surfacing what's actually converging in this specific place, and what pattern of DM's practice it represents.

Bring into the room
  • What's actually live in Spain right now, and what's the connecting thread between the pieces?
  • Is this a place worth deliberately building a coherent DM presence in, or is the activity there better read as separate, unconnected engagements?
  • What would "success" for this place-based lens look like — a demonstrator, a coalition, a documented model others can read across contexts?
Questions for the room
  • Who else in the room is working through a specific place as the unit of coherence, rather than a theme or sector — what have you learned about when that lens helps vs. when it fragments?
  • What does Spain teach us that's transferable to how DM organises around place elsewhere?

Lighter material on the table for this one — the lead should sharpen the framing above before the session, ideally the day before.

insight into strategyspread & focus

Camden Food Mission

Session 2

A cross-borough food-systems initiative with Camden Council, community food organisations and funders, built to double as a demonstrator for UK-wide food-system transformation. Organised across Supply, Hub and Demand tracks, with borough procurement as the sharpest lever — public bodies can redesign specifications rather than compete on price — and working capital plus fixed-cost cover at the hub layer as where these models actually succeed or fail.

Bring into the room
  • Where the demand side (procurement redesign) is actually ahead of or behind the hub layer's operating economics — is demand pulling faster than supply/hub can absorb?
  • The specific working-capital and fixed-cost gap at the hub — is this a bridging-finance problem, a guaranteed-offtake problem, or both?
  • What "demonstration model for UK-wide transformation" actually requires to be true beyond Camden — what has to be documented, not just delivered?
  • 2026 Patterns flags food systems as one of the fastest-rising funding areas this year — is Camden positioned to be the credible landing point for that money, or does something specific need to change first?
Questions for the room
  • Who else has tried to move a public body from competing-on-price procurement to spec-redesign — what actually got them to move?
  • Who's solved working-capital cover at an operational hub without it becoming permanent subsidy dependency?
  • What would make Camden legible as a portfolio-level proposition rather than a single-place pilot?
political economy — what people get behindcreating the conditions for pathway conversion
2026 Patterns — Pattern 7, "demand is shifting between areas of work"

Homes That Don't Cost the Earth

Session 3

A public-private-civic coalition (with Arup, UCL IIPP and Rising Tide, backed by Laudes) building the "Plan B" for housing: meeting need through existing stock — extensions, rightsizing, infill, conversions — rather than build-baby-build. The most developed piece of work on the table, with a live Theory of Change, prototype library and coalition already in motion.

Bring into the room
  • The tension between creating & convening vs. building it yourselves — where is the balance sitting today, not in theory?
  • The tactic of holding the initiative "in parts and as a whole" — which partners need the whole story, which only need their one part?
  • The Laudes co-funding math (~£550k + £450k, target €180k more in discussion) against the ask of £500–750k/year — where's the actual gap right now?
  • 2026 Patterns names housing as the sharpest-growing funding area (4% → 6% → 25% of new pathways) — but also flags this specific work as at risk of staying "in the diagnosis and solution space" when funders now want the thing tested, not the thing named. Which is it, honestly, right now?
Questions for the room
  • Have you worked on something that swung between creating and convening — how did you find the balance between effort and impact?
  • Have you acted on multi-horizons and multi-levels at once — how did you resolve conflicting visions across them?
  • Has framing "in parts and as a whole" actually helped you fundraise, or just added complexity?
structuring complex partnershipsstrategy & programme design
2026 Patterns — Pattern 4 ("paid to set things up") and Pattern 7 ("diagnosis to viability")

Beyond the Rules & Many-to-Many

Session 4

Beyond the Rules has been operating with a Lab since 2020, primarily with sequential core funding. Beyond the Rules focuses on how we organise and govern relevantly to the systems change we need to make happen. Many-to-Many is one of the strands within this, and now the primary focus of work, focusing specifically on organising and governance for multi-agent, multi-sector collaborations.

Both Beyond the Rules and Many-to-Many have gone through various cycles of Focus and Spread over the years, and have built funding opportunities primarily through field building (which later become pathways opportunities). Its initial framing blog gained lots of interest and traction when Beyond the Rules started, opening us to partnerships, collaborators, funders and speaking platforms. The focus since has been on creating consistently rigorous and high quality work and partnerships (including with edge funders in the field) and continuing to openly share our work, which has led to consistent funding despite very little pathways-building time.

The work is being applied with various demonstrators, partnerships and contexts — how it will evolve in a way that responds to the need of contexts that are strategically ripe is a question we continue to hold.

Bring into the room
  • What areas of work and governance is Many-to-Many focusing on, and what are the contexts we're applying them in, and what are we building cross-contextually (spread) in this cycle?
  • How could insights from BTR and M2M relate to other parts of DM's portfolio?
  • What have we learnt from stewarding a portfolio of work that goes through cycles of spread and focus at different times, and what it means to build a team for this?
  • What's the next stage for Beyond the Rules — spin-in, spin-out, or steady-state Lab within DM? Could/should it form a meta-frame for a wider Tooling strategy in DM?
Questions for the room
  • What are the needs in contexts people are operating in around these governance questions? Where are the areas that other contexts are most getting stuck when it comes to complex collaboration governance?
  • What vision would you hold for a next season of BTR — how do you think our next work could be as relevant as possible to world realities and needs you are seeing?
power-with relationships with partnersstructuring complex partnershipsspread & focus

City Missions

Session 5

Sits closest to DM's "dark matter" competence — the invisible systems and signals that determine where risk actually concentrates in cities, ahead of it being widely legible. Likely still in the diverging/exploratory phase rather than converged into a single demonstrator.

Bring into the room
  • What does "sensing" actually produce — a dataset, a methodology, a tool, or a relationship with the bodies who'd act on it?
  • Is this still in the spread phase (provocations, small tests) or does a condition exist to narrow into a demonstration?
  • Who is the buyer of urban risk insight, and do they currently have the mandate or budget to act on what sensing would tell them?
Questions for the room
  • Who else in the room is working with a public body that would need to change how it perceives risk before it changes how it spends?
  • Is there a piece of tooling elsewhere in DM's portfolio this should be sharing a stack with, rather than building alone?

Lighter material on the table for this one — the lead should sharpen the framing above before the session, ideally the day before.

Ladywood: 3º 2.0 & Retrofit Land Trust

Session 7

Two linked Civic Square partnership briefs, both place-based in Ladywood, both three-year programmes now entering Phase 1. 3º 2.0 revisits and updates the 3º Neighbourhoods work into risk, opportunity and vision mapping for what Ladywood — including the NPS and Retrofit Houses — needs to respond to and could become, with an eye to a replicable 3º methodology for other building sites. Retrofit Land Trust / Fairhold is a proposed ownership and tenure model, developed with Open Systems Lab, using long-term stewardship of property (via a Community Land Trust) to fund retrofit across the neighbourhood and let the community govern the outcomes — starting with the Retrofit House itself.

Bring into the room
  • Where the risk & vision mapping (3º 2.0) and the ownership & tenure model (Retrofit Land Trust) actually depend on each other — does one need the other's Phase 1 output to proceed, or can they run in parallel?
  • The replicability ambition in both briefs — a "3º methodology for building sites" and a land trust model "documented and networked for replication" — what would make Ladywood a genuine template rather than a one-off?
  • Both are DM-Civic Square rate-aligned day-rate budgets (£563/day) against a fairly open Phase 2–3 co-funding ask — where's the real funding gap sitting right now?
Questions for the room
  • Who else has translated a values-led framework (like the six 3º reimaginings) into decisions a design team or council will actually act on?
  • Who's worked on a Community Land Trust or comparable long-term stewardship vehicle — what did the Phase 1 "problem definition" need to contain to survive into a real Phase 2 legal set-up?
  • What's the retrospective version of a neighbourhood-scale demonstrator that didn't make it to replication — what actually stopped it travelling?

The layer of DM's funding stack where a proven position becomes an actual investable deal — currently the one layer with dedicated resourcing, sitting above Coordination Tooling and the unfunded Precursor layer that DM has always run on borrowed capacity rather than a funded structure of its own.

Bring into the room

Convergence — naming the three areas of craft

There's already a working brainstorm of candidate craft areas, and 2026 Patterns adds a few more worth testing. The job this afternoon is not to invent new ones, but to converge the room's actual signal — from the ten deep dives just run — down to the three that matter most to go deep on Wednesday.

Retrospective on where it really hasn't worked Power-with relationships with partners Structuring complex partnerships Strategy & programme design From problem to opposing pathways to an option Cross-team organising Creating the conditions for good pathway conversion Managing relevance & overwhelm Political economy — what people will get behind Insight gifs of each other's strategies Agreeing what we say yes to & distributing capacity Evidencing what we've actually built Getting paid to set things up, not just deliver Clean handovers & promise-keeping

Amber chips are new candidates surfaced in 2026 Patterns — see Patterns 2, 3, 4 & 5 — not yet tested against this room's actual deep-dive signal.

1

Cluster the wall (20 min)

Bring every craft-signal card from the day's three Spaces and the chip list above together on one wall. In small mixed groups, cluster cards that are naming the same underlying craft, even if worded differently.

2

Name the clusters (20 min)

Each group gives their clusters a plain-language name and a one-line test: "you'd know you had this craft if you could ___." Post on the wall.

3

Dot-vote (15 min)

Three dots each, weighted by "which craft, if we don't build it, most limits what today's ten pieces of work can become." Not popularity — capability gap.

4

Stress-test the top three (25 min)

For the top three by vote, one person argues against including it ("this is really a symptom of the craft above it, not its own craft") before the room commits. This catches false convergence.

5

Craft Confidence Map (10 min)

Against each of the three named craft areas, everyone marks how confident they feel holding it — not to rank people, but so the room has an honest picture of who feels strong where. Used directly to build Wednesday's studios: a mix of confidence levels in each room, not just whoever's most enthusiastic. Also the starting point for a longer-term answer to "who feels confident in which part of the craft, so we can support each other more across the org."

Wednesday — Craft & Tooling

By Wednesday, the three areas of craft that actually matter aren't a guess — they've come straight out of Monday's deep dives, tested against ten live pieces of work rather than picked in the abstract. That clarity is what lets this day go deep rather than broad: two full rounds of craft practice, a cross-studio exchange, and space to opt in to what leadership actually asks of us next.

✎

The three craft areas land live. Rather than fix them in advance, the studios below are named from Monday afternoon's card sort and dot-vote (see the Monday page). Whatever the room converges on — from candidates like power-with partnerships, political economy, strategy & programme design, managing relevance & overwhelm, or the newer 2026 Patterns candidates like evidencing our work or getting paid to set things up — gets its own studio here. Craft Studios — Round 1

One studio per craft area named on Monday. Each studio is a working session, not a lecture — it should leave with something usable, not just a shared vocabulary.

1

Ground the craft in the team's own insight (15 min)

Each studio opens with whichever of the team's own strategy insights bears most directly on their craft — requisite variety and the tension with focus; resonance ("we attract what we are"); the builder/driver/enabler split; spread & focus as recurring phases; spin-in/spin-out as an explicit trajectory; the reminder that the posture you build a relationship with is the posture that embeds.

2

Craft Clinic (50 min)

Action-learning format. Each person brings one live decision — ideally one that surfaced during Monday's deep dives — that this craft bears on. In turn: 5 min to present the decision, 5 min of clarifying questions only (no advice), 10 min of the group offering what they'd try, 2 min for the presenter to say what landed. Rotate through as many people as time allows.

3

First pass at an artefact (10 min)

Before the break, each studio drafts — doesn't finish — one concrete thing this craft needs to exist: a checklist, a term sheet clause, a one-page retrospective template, a partnership MOU pattern. Round 2 sharpens it.

Craft Studios — Round 2

Same studio, same craft, a second run at it — now with a working draft to sharpen rather than a blank page.

4

Craft Clinic, round two (45 min)

Run again with whoever didn't get a turn in Round 1, or return to the hardest case from Round 1 with fresh eyes. If the studio's craft is genuinely contested (e.g. does a Many-to-Many contract fit a power-with posture, or pull against it?), spend this round on that tension directly rather than another round of individual cases.

5

Finish the artefact (20 min)

Take the Round 1 draft to something an owner could actually use next week. Name who owns finishing it properly within two weeks, and who it's for.

6

Prep the swap (5 min)

Choose one person to stay and host the studio's artefact during the Craft Swap; everyone else visits another studio.

Craft Swap — cross-studio exchange

The step that stops each craft studio becoming its own silo. A deliberate structure for cross-pollination, not just a shared lunch.

Move

One host stays

Each studio leaves one person behind with the artefact and a two-minute pitch. Everyone else moves to a different studio.

Ask

Stress-test, not admire

Visitors' job is to ask "where would this break on my piece of work?" — not to compliment the artefact.

Return

Bring one edit home

Everyone returns to their own studio with one concrete edit gathered from outside it, and folds it in before the artefact is called done.

Opting in to leadership

What does our mission need of us, and how do we respond to it with integrity? This is the session where the pop-up turns from craft toward personal commitment.

Exercise

Skin in the Game, revisited

Return to Tuesday's spectrum line on "we have skin in the game where it matters." Stand on it again, individually this time, for your own piece of work specifically — not DM in the abstract. Notice what moved and what didn't.

Exercise

The Leadership Letter

15 minutes, written, addressed to the team: what am I opting into for the coming season, given what I now know about the craft this work actually needs? Sealed and handed to a peer to return in three months, not read aloud today.

Closing — harvest & commitments

1

Craft artefact readout (20 min)

Each studio reads out its finished artefact and its owner — into the room, into the record, not just onto a wall.

2

Closing circle (10 min)

One sentence each: what I'm taking back to my piece of work from these four days. No cross-talk, no response — just witnessed.

Depart from 3:30pm.

Craft Studio Options

Only three craft areas get a studio this time. These are other candidates, drafted from the Pre-Read and 2026 Patterns — not deep dives into a piece of work, but craft and tooling worth building next: a checklist, a protocol, a practice. Parked here for a future studio, not scheduled today.

Ten craft studio options, in four clusters

Getting better at money

Patterns · Pattern 3

Evidencing What We've Built

Funders buy proof now, and it's our weakest line. Build the thing that actually makes our impact legible — checkable claims, progress shown as it happens — instead of another report.

Patterns · Pattern 4

Getting Paid to Set Things Up

Four pieces of work this year were us organising, not delivering — and we still price it in day rates. Design the alternative: a stewardship retainer, a convening fee, a share of what gets mobilised.

Patterns · Pattern 6

Match-Funding as the Entry Condition

Flagged in the Patterns as genuinely unresolved. Turn "match funding isn't a bonus any more" into an actual practice for how we approach funders.

Getting better at how we work together

Patterns · Pattern 2

Agreeing What We Say Yes To

Good individual refusals this year, no shared basis for them. Build the shared test for partner fit, and who decides when capacity moves from one partner to another.

Patterns · Pattern 5

Clean Handovers & Promise-Keeping

Three over-budget projects this year share a pattern: what was promised never reached the people delivering it. Draft the short protocol — what's promised, at what price, with what latitude, who can authorise going over.

Getting better at where we point ourselves

Patterns · Pattern 1

A Test for Entering Open Calls

Turn the starting hunch — do we already hold the funder, is there a direct-award route, do we have someone who can carry it to contract — into an actual checklist.

Patterns · Pattern 7

Following the Money as It Moves

Housing, risk & security, AI/digital, food and oceans are all rising; nature-based finance and broad everything-at-once framings are falling. Build the practice of spotting that shift early, not reading it a year later.

Pre-Read · Our landscape

Refreshing the Landscape Matrix

The matrix, the craft spiral and the locations-&-partners view are all named as pending in the Pre-Read. Worth a session to actually move them from pending to done.

Getting better at telling our own story

Pre-Read

Stories of Our Work in Practice

Flagged as "still to come": clearer stories about what we're doing, including where it worked, where it didn't, and what that taught us.

Pre-Read

Building the Learning & Information-Flow System

Named directly as something we still need, rather than something we should assume already exists.

Reference

Facilitation Toolkit

Quick reference for every exercise named across the four days, so whoever's holding the room doesn't have to hunt back through the agenda.

✎

How to use this page. Each card names the day and format it's used in on the main agenda pages — this is the "how it works" reference to keep on hand while actually running the session.

All the exercises

Monday · Per-session

The Overview Format

Tight two-part structure for each session: what it is and why it matters now, then one live question the lead actually wants help with. Keeps every ~20-minute overview comparable even though the content differs wildly.

Monday · Convergence

Card Sort & Dot-Vote

Cluster raw signals into named groups, then vote with a constrained number of dots against a specific test ("which gap most limits the work"), not general preference.

Monday · Convergence

Stress-Test the Shortlist

Before locking in a converged decision, assign someone to argue against each finalist. Catches convergence that happened for social reasons rather than real signal.

Wednesday · Small group

Craft Clinic (action-learning set)

Structured peer consultation: present, clarify, offer, close. Rotates through several real decisions rather than going deep on one — built for volume of practical traction, not therapy-depth reflection. Run twice on Wednesday, with an artefact sharpened between rounds.

Wednesday · Cross-group

Craft Swap

One host stays with each group's artefact while everyone else visits a different group to stress-test it. Forces contact between craft areas that would otherwise stay siloed in their own room all day.

Wednesday · Individual

The Leadership Letter

Private written commitment, sealed and returned later rather than read aloud — lowers performance pressure and makes the commitment genuinely personal.

A working principle, if you need it mid-session

"The best strategies are formed dialogically with the field, possible funders and other partners. If we advance strategies alone they often quickly die."
